headline_marked: Hasan up 26 places as [[Tigers surge in ICC Test rankings]] after Darwin win
headline: Hasan up 26 places as Tigers surge in ICC Test rankings after Darwin win
summary: Following a sensational nine-wicket victory over Australia, Bangladesh's red-ball stars make significant gains in the latest ICC Men's Test Player Rankings.
details: Bangladesh's red-ball stars have been rewarded for their remarkable nine-wicket victory over Australia in the first Test in Darwin, making big gains in the latest ICC Men's Test Player Rankings.
Hasan Mahmud was the big mover among bowlers, jumping 26 places to 38th after picking up nine wickets across the match and being named Player of the Match.
Skipper Najmul Hossain Shanto rose nine places to 20th in the batters' rankings following an excellent first-innings score of 84.
Other gains include Mehidy Hasan, who moved up three spots to 24th after a five-wicket haul in the second innings, and Mominul Haque, who climbed five rungs to 31st.
In a major shift, Australia's Travis Head relinquished his spot as the top-ranked Test batter, dropping three places to fourth overall.
England's Harry Brook has reclaimed the top position, followed by teammates Joe Root and Australia's Steve Smith.
The rankings remain tight, with only 33 rating points separating the top four batters, suggesting further movement is likely in upcoming series.
caption:
Hasan Mahmud jumps 26 places! 🚀 The Tigers' historic win in Darwin has triggered a massive surge in the ICC Test rankings.

Bangladesh's red-ball stars have been rewarded for their remarkable nine-wicket victory over Australia in the first Test in Darwin, making big gains in the latest ICC Men's Test Player Rankings.

Hasan Mahmud was the big mover among bowlers, jumping 26 places to 38th after picking up nine wickets across the match and being named Player of the Match.

Skipper Najmul Hossain Shanto rose nine places to 20th in the batters' rankings following an excellent first-innings score of 84.

Other gains include Mehidy Hasan, who moved up three spots to 24th after a five-wicket haul in the second innings, and Mominul Haque, who climbed five rungs to 31st.

In a major shift, Australia's Travis Head relinquished his spot as the top-ranked Test batter, dropping three places to fourth overall.

England's Harry Brook has reclaimed the top position, followed by teammates Joe Root and Australia's Steve Smith.

The rankings remain tight, with only 33 rating points separating the top four batters, suggesting further movement is likely in upcoming series.

headline_marked: Law experts urge [[agencies cannot investigate themselves]] in disappearance cases
headline: Law experts urge agencies cannot investigate themselves in disappearance cases
summary: Former ICT chief prosecutor Tajul Islam and rights activists warn that proposed laws may allow law enforcement to avoid accountability for enforced disappearances.
details: Former International Crimes Tribunal chief prosecutor Tajul Islam has warned that law enforcement agencies accused of enforced disappearances should not be allowed to investigate their own members.
Speaking at a roundtable in Dhaka, Tajul urged the government to reconsider the proposed laws on enforced disappearance and the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) before they are passed.
He emphasized that courts cannot ensure justice if investigations are flawed, as judges can only adjudicate based on the evidence presented to them.

Dr Nabila Idris, a former member of the Commission of Inquiry on Enforced Disappearances, noted that proposed laws for the NHRC and the Special Response Battalion (SRB) also contain restrictions on independent investigations.
Under the proposed disappearance law, complaints must be lodged with police officers, which Dr Nabila argued creates a conflict of interest since police personnel themselves are often the accused.

She revealed that while the disappearance commission received over 1,500 complaints, evidence was found in only about 250 cases, partly because police often refused to record complaints against their own.
Rights activist Nur Khan Liton added that the NHRC would remain ineffective unless its members possess the necessary competence, integrity, and courage to conduct independent probes.
The event, organized by Voice for Reform and Nagorik Coalition, was attended by victims' families and various human rights advocates.
caption:
Can law enforcement investigate their own crimes? Experts warn that proposed laws may let agencies avoid accountability for disappearances.

Former International Crimes Tribunal chief prosecutor Tajul Islam has warned that law enforcement agencies accused of enforced disappearances should not be allowed to investigate their own members.

Speaking at a roundtable in Dhaka, Tajul urged the government to reconsider the proposed laws on enforced disappearance and the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) before they are passed.

He emphasized that courts cannot ensure justice if investigations are flawed, as judges can only adjudicate based on the evidence presented to them.

Dr Nabila Idris, a former member of the Commission of Inquiry on Enforced Disappearances, noted that proposed laws for the NHRC and the Special Response Battalion (SRB) also contain restrictions on independent investigations.

Under the proposed disappearance law, complaints must be lodged with police officers, which Dr Nabila argued creates a conflict of interest since police personnel themselves are often the accused.

She revealed that while the disappearance commission received over 1,500 complaints, evidence was found in only about 250 cases, partly because police often refused to record complaints against their own.

Rights activist Nur Khan Liton added that the NHRC would remain ineffective unless its members possess the necessary competence, integrity, and courage to conduct independent probes.

The event, organized by Voice for Reform and Nagorik Coalition, was attended by victims' families and various human rights advocates.
